name: MVCC Snapshot Isolation, Tuple Versioning & Write-Skew Prevention
tagline: Understand how MVCC keeps reads non-blocking via (xmin, xmax) tuple chains, why Snapshot Isolation suffers Write Skew, and how SSI eliminates it.
purpose: Master MVCC visibility rules, Write-Skew anomalies on disjoint rows, Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), and 40001 retry handling.

spark.summary: MVCC lets readers and writers run lock-free via (xmin, xmax) tuple versions, but Snapshot Isolation allows Write Skew on disjoint rows unless guarded by SSI (40001 retries) or parent locks.
spark.keyTakeaway: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, tuple Versioning & Write-Skew Prevention, snapshot Isolation only catches write-write conflicts on the same row—use SERIALIZABLE (SSI) with bounded 40001 retries or materialize a shared lock row to enforce multi-row invariants.
spark.byteSummary:
Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) lets database readers and writers operate concurrently without blocking one another: instead of overwriting rows in place, each `UPDATE` appends a new tuple version tagged with `(xmin, xmax)` transaction IDs. A reader running under `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation) simply reads the latest tuple version visible at its transaction start snapshot (`xmin <= snap < xmax`), guaranteeing a consistent point-in-time view with zero read locks.

However, Snapshot Isolation (SI) has a subtle, dangerous blind spot called **Write Skew**. When two concurrent transactions read an overlapping premise (e.g., `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM on_call WHERE active = true` returns `2`) and then mutate **disjoint rows** (`Alice` sets `Alice.active = false`; `Bob` sets `Bob.active = false`), neither transaction triggers a row-level write-write conflict. Both commit cleanly—leaving `0` engineers on call and silently violating the business invariant.

Closing Write Skew requires either **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**—which tracks `SIREAD` predicate locks and aborts `rw-antidependency` cycles with SQLSTATE `40001`—or explicit lock materialization (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a shared parent row, or `EXCLUDE USING GIST` constraints). Every SSI caller must wrap transactions in a bounded, jittered retry loop for `40001 serialization_failure`.

learningJourney.title: Non-Blocking Reads via (xmin, xmax) Tuple Version Chains
learningJourney.purpose: Explain how PostgreSQL MVCC keeps concurrent readers and writers non-blocking using immutable tuple versions.

explanation.foundation: In a locking-only database, long analytical reads block writers and writers block readers. MVCC avoids this by keeping multiple versions of each logical row: `xmin` records the inserting transaction ID and `xmax` records the deleting/updating transaction ID.
explanation.core: When transaction `tx=102` opens a snapshot, it sees Tuple `v1` (`xmin=100, xmax=105`) even after `tx=105` inserts `v2` (`xmin=105, xmax=inf`). Readers never acquire row locks and writers never wait on readers.
explanation.deepDive: PostgreSQL stores old and new tuple versions directly in heap pages (requiring `VACUUM` to reclaim dead tuples), whereas InnoDB/MySQL stores current rows in the clustered index and reconstructs older snapshots from the Undo Log.

learningJourney.title: Why Disjoint-Row Updates Bypass Snapshot Isolation Locks
learningJourney.purpose: Trace how two transactions reading the same premise and updating different rows violate invariants under Snapshot Isolation.

explanation.foundation: Snapshot Isolation (PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ`) prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and lost updates on the **same row** via the First-Committer-Wins rule.
explanation.core: Write Skew occurs when Tx A and Tx B read a shared set (`count = 2` on-call), then Tx A updates Row `Alice` while Tx B updates Row `Bob`. Because their write sets are disjoint, First-Committer-Wins sees zero conflict—and both commit, leaving `0` on call.
explanation.deepDive: Write Skew also hits double-booking calendars (two non-overlapping checks on overlapping time ranges), bank overdrafts across paired checking+savings accounts, and unique-claim workflows lacking a unique constraint.

sectionDiagram.title: Why Disjoint-Row Updates Bypass Snapshot Isolation Locks

cards.label: Disjoint Write Sets
cards.detail: Row-level write locks only catch conflicts when two transactions modify the exact same primary key.

cards.label: Silent Corruption
cards.detail: PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ returns 200 OK to both callers with zero error.

cards.label: Multi-Row Invariants
cards.detail: Any constraint spanning >1 row (e.g., sum >= 0, count >= 1, no time overlap) is vulnerable under SI.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement MVCC Snapshot Isolation, Tuple Versioning & Write-Skew Prevention without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, tuple Versioning & Write-Skew Prevention, snapshot Isolation only catches write-write conflicts on the same row—use SERIALIZABLE (SSI) with bounded 40001 retries or materialize a shared lock row to enforce multi-row invariants.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: Detecting rw-Antidependency Cycles with SIREAD Predicate Locks
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate Write Skew optimistically using PostgreSQL SSI's SIREAD locks without blocking readers.

explanation.foundation: `ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE` in PostgreSQL uses **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**—it still never blocks readers with traditional 2PL.
explanation.core: Instead, SSI attaches lightweight **SIREAD predicate locks** to tuples and index pages read by each transaction. When Tx A writes a row matching Tx B's SIREAD set (and vice versa), SSI detects a dangerous `rw-antidependency` cycle.
explanation.deepDive: The moment two consecutive `rw-antidependency` edges form a cycle, SSI aborts the second committer with SQLSTATE `40001` (`could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`), preserving strict serializability.

sectionDiagram.title: Detecting rw-Antidependency Cycles with SIREAD Predicate Locks

nodes.label: rw-Antidependency
nodes.sub: Tx A Reads -> Tx B Writes

nodes.label: Cycle Detected
nodes.sub: Tx A <-> Tx B Mutual rw

cards.label: Optimistic Detection
cards.detail: SIREAD locks never block queries—they only track potential serialization anomalies until commit.

cards.label: False Positives Possible
cards.detail: Page/index-level SIREAD granularity means unrelated rows on the same B-tree page can occasionally trigger 40001.

cards.label: Mandatory Retry
cards.detail: Applications using SERIALIZABLE must treat SQLSTATE 40001 as a normal retryable signal, not a fatal 500.

learningJourney.title: Bounded Jittered 40001 Retry Loop for SSI Transactions
learningJourney.purpose: Wrap SERIALIZABLE transactions in a bounded exponential-backoff + jitter retry loop that rolls back cleanly on 40001.

explanation.foundation: Calling a `SERIALIZABLE` transaction once without retrying `40001` turns normal concurrency into user-facing errors.
explanation.core:
```python
import random
import time

def run_ssi_with_retry(conn, fn, max_attempts: int = 5):
    if max_attempts <= 0:
        raise ValueError('max_attempts must be positive')
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            with conn.cursor() as cur:
                cur.execute('BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE')
                result = fn(cur)
                cur.execute('COMMIT')
                return result
        except Exception as exc:
            conn.rollback()
            if getattr(exc, 'sqlstate', None) == '40001' and attempt + 1 < max_attempts:
                sleep_s = (0.01 * (2 ** attempt)) * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)
                time.sleep(sleep_s)
                continue
            raise
```
explanation.deepDive: Always execute `conn.rollback()` before sleeping so the failed transaction releases its snapshot and SIREAD locks immediately, and keep `fn(cur)` free of external HTTP side effects that would duplicate on retry.

sectionDiagram.title: Bounded Jittered 40001 Retry Loop for SSI Transactions

cards.label: Pure DB Closure
cards.detail: Never send emails or charge cards inside fn(cur)—use a transactional outbox row instead.

cards.label: Explicit Rollback
cards.detail: Rolling back before sleeping frees virtual XIDs and SIREAD memory immediately.

cards.label: Full Jitter
cards.detail: Randomizing backoff prevents two colliding transactions from retrying in lockstep.

sectionDiagram.summary: Rolling back immediately on 40001 and retrying pure DB closures with jittered backoff makes SSI production-safe.

learningJourney.title: SSI vs. Parent-Row Materialization vs. GiST Exclusion Constraints
learningJourney.purpose: Choose between SSI, SELECT FOR UPDATE on a parent lock row, and PostgreSQL EXCLUDE constraints under high contention.

explanation.foundation: Under 5% contention, SSI shines with zero lock waits. Under 80% contention on a single shift, optimistic 40001 retries waste CPU.
explanation.core: Materializing a parent `shift_buckets(shift_id, oncall_count)` row and locking it with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` serializes contention in a single FIFO queue—zero wasted rollbacks.
explanation.deepDive: For calendar/booking overlap invariants, PostgreSQL `EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)` enforces non-overlap at the index level even under `READ COMMITTED`.

sectionDiagram.title: SSI vs. Parent-Row Materialization vs. GiST Exclusion Constraints

cards.label: Optimistic vs. Pessimistic
cards.detail: SSI avoids locks when conflicts are rare; SELECT FOR UPDATE avoids retry storms when conflicts are frequent.

cards.label: Index-Level Guarantees
cards.detail: EXCLUDE USING gist prevents overlapping reservations inside the B-tree/GiST index itself.

cards.label: Hybrid Pattern
cards.detail: Use READ COMMITTED + parent-row lock for hot shifts, or SSI for cross-table business rules.

sectionDiagram.summary: Matching SSI, parent-row locking, or GiST exclusion constraints to contention levels avoids rollback storms.
sectionDiagram.caption: Matching SSI, parent-row locking, or GiST exclusion constraints to contention levels avoids rollback storms.

learningJourney.title: Isolating Long-Running Snapshots & SIREAD Lock Memory Exhaustion
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent long-running analytics transactions from pinning dead tuples and exhausting shared predicate lock memory.

explanation.foundation: An idle-in-transaction session holding an old MVCC snapshot prevents `VACUUM` from reclaiming dead tuples across the entire database.
explanation.core: Enforce `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '15s'` and `statement_timeout = '5s'` on OLTP pools, and route BI queries to a dedicated read replica with `hot_standby_feedback = off`.
explanation.deepDive: In PostgreSQL, `max_pred_locks_per_transaction` (default 64) controls shared-memory SIREAD slots; if thousands of concurrent SSI transactions touch many pages, SIREAD locks escalate to coarse relation locks—increasing 40001 false positives.

sectionDiagram.title: Isolating Long-Running Snapshots & SIREAD Lock Memory Exhaustion

cards.label: Global xmin Pinning
cards.detail: One forgotten BEGIN; in a developer psql shell can bloat a 500 GB table during peak traffic.

cards.label: SIREAD Escalation
cards.detail: Too-small max_pred_locks_per_transaction causes page locks to escalate to whole-table locks, spiking 40001s.

cards.label: Replica Offload
cards.detail: Keep analytical scans off the OLTP primary so short OLTP snapshots stay fast.

sectionDiagram.summary: Idle-in-transaction timeouts, replica offloading, and tuned SIREAD lock tables prevent MVCC bloat and false aborts.
sectionDiagram.caption: Idle-in-transaction timeouts, replica offloading, and tuned SIREAD lock tables prevent MVCC bloat and false aborts.

learningJourney.title: Tracking 40001 Retry Rates, Dead-Tuple Ratios & xmin Age
learningJourney.purpose: Monitor serialization abort ratios, exhausted retry budgets, and oldest-snapshot age in real time.

explanation.foundation: Silent retry storms can double database CPU long before 5xx errors appear in API logs.
explanation.deepDive: Alert if `40001` retry rate exceeds 5% of total commits (signaling a hot predicate that needs parent-row locking) or if `max_tx_xmin_age_seconds > 300s`.

knowledgeChecks.question: Under PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ (Snapshot Isolation), Alice and Bob are both on call (count=2). Simultaneously, Tx A checks `count >= 2` and sets `Alice.on_call = false`, while Tx B checks `count >= 2` and sets `Bob.on_call = false`. What happens?

options.text: PostgreSQL aborts Tx B with a serialization failure because both read the same table.
options.feedback: REPEATABLE READ does not track SIREAD predicate locks—only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) does.

options.text: Both transactions commit cleanly because they updated disjoint rows, leaving 0 engineers on call (Write Skew).
options.feedback: Correct! Snapshot Isolation's First-Committer-Wins rule only catches conflicts on the exact same row.

options.text: Tx B blocks until Tx A commits, then re-evaluates count and sees 1.
options.feedback: Snapshot readers and disjoint-row writers do not block each other under REPEATABLE READ.

options.text: PostgreSQL automatically rolls back both transactions as a deadlock.
options.feedback: There is no lock cycle here—both transactions update separate rows without blocking.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Snapshot Isolation permits disjoint-row updates from overlapping snapshots, producing the Write-Skew anomaly.

knowledgeChecks.question: How does PostgreSQL Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) prevent Write Skew without blocking concurrent SELECT queries?

options.text: It converts every SELECT into a blocking table-level exclusive lock.
options.feedback: SSI never blocks readers; it uses optimistic conflict detection.

options.text: It tracks non-blocking SIREAD predicate locks and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 when an rw-antidependency cycle forms.
options.feedback: Correct! SIREAD locks record what each transaction read and detect dangerous rw-cycles at commit time.

options.text: It disables MVCC and forces all transactions to run single-threaded.
options.feedback: SSI runs fully concurrently on top of MVCC.

options.text: It deletes old tuple versions immediately on every UPDATE.
options.feedback: MVCC tuple retention and VACUUM still operate normally under SSI.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: SSI pairs MVCC snapshots with non-blocking SIREAD predicate locks, aborting rw-antidependency cycles with 40001.

knowledgeChecks.question: A 4-hour analytical query runs in an `idle in transaction` session on the primary OLTP database. What operational failure does this trigger?

options.text: It prevents VACUUM from reclaiming dead tuples newer than that session's xmin snapshot, causing severe table bloat.
options.feedback: Correct! Old open snapshots pin the global xmin horizon, blocking dead-tuple cleanup.

options.text: It immediately corrupts B-tree indexes on all tables.
options.feedback: Snapshots do not corrupt indexes; they pin dead tuple reclamation.

options.text: It forces all other sessions to downgrade to READ UNCOMMITTED.
options.feedback: Other sessions retain their configured isolation levels.

options.text: It resets the database transaction ID counter back to 0.
options.feedback: Transaction IDs continue advancing; old snapshots actually increase wraparound urgency.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Long-lived snapshots pin the global xmin horizon, preventing VACUUM from reclaiming dead MVCC tuple versions.
